statement: Jura is a compact eastern French wine region whose six wine AOPs form three overlapping families: geographic still-wine origins, traditional-method Crémant du Jura, and fortified Macvin du Jura.

Jura makes legal hierarchy, grape identity and winemaking method unusually easy to compare in one small place: Chardonnay and Savagnin whites, three red grapes, vin jaune, sparkling wine and mistelle all coexist without meaning the same thing.
The Jura vineyard forms a narrow north–south band along the western foothills of the Jura mountains, with varied slopes and exposures rather than one uniform site.
Arbois, Côtes du Jura, L’Etoile and Château-Chalon are geographic AOPs; Crémant du Jura and Macvin du Jura overlap that geography but govern different wine categories and methods.

Côtes du Jura permits white, red, rosé and vin jaune; Crémant du Jura is traditional-method sparkling wine; Macvin du Jura is a white, red or rosé liqueur wine. These are distinct legal styles, not interchangeable labels.

Burgundy is a long, fragmented wine region whose identity is read through nested origin: regional appellations, village wines, Premier Cru sites and Grand Cru appellations.
Burgundy makes origin hierarchy visible: a modest change in named place can change legal category, expected scale and how a learner should read the bottle.
BIVB reports a production split of 53% regional appellations, 46% village and Premier Cru appellations, and 1% Grand Cru appellations on its stated five-year-average basis.

The Loire Valley is a long river-linked wine world, not one compact vineyard: Atlantic Muscadet, Anjou-Saumur and Touraine lead east toward Centre-Loire, with changing climate, soils, grapes and appellations.
Loire teaches range: still and sparkling, dry and sweet, white, red and rosé wines emerge from a river corridor where no single grape or soil explains the whole region.
Follow the Loire and its tributaries west to east, but expect geology and maritime influence to change along the route; the river connects the wine world without making it uniform.

Beaujolais is a 12-AOC region built around two broad appellations and ten northern crus, with Gamay at its center but meaningful differences in geology, exposure and origin.
Beaujolais shows how one dominant grape can still yield a region of distinct places: broad Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages context surrounds ten individually named crus.
The ten crus occupy the northern half of the region; Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages provide the broader appellation frame and can include red, white and rosé wines.
Official regional soil research identified hundreds of soil variants across a geologically complex region; Beaujolais should not be reduced to a single granite-soil story.

Béarn is the historical and cultural foothill world around Pau; CARTA keeps it distinct from Béarn AOP and uses Jurançon as the clearest mapped route into its white-wine culture.
The Béarn–Jurançon world makes the relationship between mountain foothills, long autumn ripening, local Manseng grapes and both dry and sweet white wine unusually legible.
INAO describes hillside vineyards in the Pyrenean foothills under oceanic influence, with a warm dry southerly autumn wind that can support ripening and concentration.
Jurançon includes dry and sweet white-wine traditions centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng; sweetness is a style distinction inside the appellation, not a different geography.

Arbois is a geographic Jura AOP with a broad still-wine range, including white, red, rosé, vin jaune and vin de paille traditions.
Côtes du Jura is the broad geographic Jura AOP and supports white, red, rosé, vin jaune and vin de paille under its own rules.
Château-Chalon is a small geographic Jura AOP devoted to vin jaune from Savagnin; it is not a synonym for every Jura vin jaune.
L’Etoile is a small geographic Jura AOP centered on white-wine traditions, including vin jaune and vin de paille.
Crémant du Jura governs traditional-method sparkling wine across geography that overlaps the region’s still-wine origins.
Macvin du Jura is a white, red or rosé liqueur wine under its own AOP, not a still-wine origin shorthand or a synonym for vin jaune.
Morgon is one of the ten northern Beaujolais crus, with Gamay at its center and a distinct regulatory geographic area.
Vouvray is a right-bank Loire AOP centered on Chenin Blanc and spanning dry, demi-sec, moelleux and sparkling wine styles.
Jurançon is a Pyrenean-foothill white-wine AOP centered on Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng, with established dry and sweet traditions.
